props.title: Raw Force

sections.content: Raw Force (1982) stands as a gloriously unhinged exploitation mashup that throws everything into the blender - martial arts, zombies, cannibals, and sleazy action. It follows the "Burbank Kung Fu Club" to a mysterious island where disgraced martial artists face off against zombie warriors raised by evil monks. The film shares DNA with Enter the Dragon (1973) and grindhouse classics like Zombie Flesh Eaters (1979), while prefiguring the anything-goes attitude of later B-movies like Miami Connection (1987).

sections.content: The early 1980s saw an explosion of genre-blending martial arts films trying to capitalize on the kung fu craze while adding supernatural elements. The Boxer's Omen (1983) went full psychedelic horror with black magic and monster battles, while Ninja III: The Domination (1984) somehow merged ninja action with possession horror and aerobics. These films reflected both the martial arts boom and exploitation producers' need to stand out in a crowded market.

Raw Force particularly excels in its gleefully tasteless approach, throwing in gratuitous nudity, violence, and politically incorrect humor that would never fly today. Director Edward D. Murphy, who only directed one other film, creates a perfect storm of exploitation elements that makes this a standout in the "so bad it's good" category alongside films like Hard Ticket to Hawaii (1987) and Samurai Cop (1991). sections.content: The film's influence can be seen in later tongue-in-cheek martial arts films like Miami Connection (1987) and Deadly Prey (1987), which similarly embrace their low-budget roots while piling on excessive violence and outlandish plots. Modern filmmakers like Robert Rodriguez and Quentin Tarantino have openly acknowledged their debt to these types of exploitation films, with Planet Terror (2007) and Kill Bill Vol. 1 (2003) serving as loving homages to the genre.
